Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.

summaries.gardner: Visa has several Rule Breaker traits: a dominant brand, strong management and a network that keeps growing, but it is a mature incumbent rather than a top dog in an emerging industry. Its shares rose about 15% over the last year, trailing the S&P 500, so the momentum trait is missing.
summaries.buffett: Visa fits Buffett's tenets closely: a simple toll-road business, net revenue up every year from $21,846M (FY2020) to $40,000M (FY2025), returns on capital above 50% and free cash flow above net income. The main gap is price: at about 34 times trailing earnings there is little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Visa is the kind of wonderful business Munger favoured, a two-sided network with roughly 60% operating margins that is hard to dislodge. Inverting, the main ways it could fail are regulation (the 2024 DOJ debit suit, routing mandates) and government or bank-backed account-to-account rails, which are real but slow-moving.
summaries.lynch: Visa is a stalwart with fast-grower traits: earnings per share grew from $2.58 in FY2015 to $10.20 in FY2025. Lynch's price tests are not met, since a P/E near 34 is well above its low-to-mid-teens earnings growth, insiders are net sellers and the stock is widely owned.
summaries.fisher: Visa scores well on Fisher's points: a long runway in digital payments, steady new products (tokenization, Visa Direct, Visa Intelligent Commerce), high margins and strong sales relationships with issuers. The weaker points are that its R&D is not separately prominent and management is professional rather than founder-led.
summaries.graham: Visa fails most of Graham's defensive tests on price: about 42 times three-year average earnings and P/E times P/B above 700, far above 22.5. It is large and profitable every year, but it has paid dividends only since its 2008 IPO, short of Graham's 20-year record.
summaries.thiel: Visa is a near-monopoly network (with Mastercard) that has strong distribution through thousands of banks and durable network effects. It does not answer Thiel's questions about a new, 10x technology or a secret that others miss, because it is a 60-year-old incumbent.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable compounders with clear catalysts at reasonable prices; Visa compounds revenue in the low teens with exposure to agentic commerce and stablecoin settlement. Its valuation of about 27 times forward earnings and lagging share price over the past year make it a quality hold rather than a high-conviction rerating story.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller focuses on liquidity, earnings momentum and price trends; Visa's earnings are steady rather than accelerating sharply and its share price has trailed the market over the past year. It is a defensive compounder rather than the kind of macro-driven, concentrated bet he typically makes.
summaries.smith: Visa is a textbook Terry Smith holding: very high returns on capital (ROIC about 55%), gross margin near 98%, strong cash conversion and growth from the shift away from cash. The question for Smith would be only whether a free-cash-flow yield of about 2.9% is too much to pay.
summaries.greenblatt: Visa ranks very high on return on capital but poorly on earnings yield: EV/EBIT of about 25 implies an earnings yield near 4%. That combination would not put it near the top of the Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: Visa fits all three legs of Akre's stool: an extraordinary business, skilled and shareholder-minded management, and room to reinvest via new flows and value-added services. Akre's fund has long owned Visa and Mastercard for exactly these reasons, though most of Visa's cash is returned rather than reinvested.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks simple businesses bought cheaply during temporary distress with low downside risk; Visa is simple and low-risk but not distressed or cheap. It would only fit his approach after a sharp, temporary sell-off, for example on a regulatory scare.
summaries.wood: Visa is not an ARK-style disruptive innovator; it is more often cast as an incumbent at risk from blockchain, stablecoins and real-time payments. Its own moves into stablecoin settlement and AI-agent payments give it some exposure to ARK themes, but it is not a leader in them.
summaries.ackman: Visa matches Ackman's criteria for a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative business with a dominant position and high barriers to entry. Pershing Square is not known as a Visa holder, and the current price leaves limited upside by his standards.
summaries.sleep: Visa has scale economics, but it keeps most of the benefit as margin rather than sharing it with customers as Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model prefers. Its position in 10–20 years looks durable but not clearly stronger, given regulatory and alternative-rails pressure.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and products that solve painful problems; Visa solves the painful problem of trusted payments at global scale. As a mature public company it is far from the early-stage, market-creating ventures Sequoia backed.
summaries.nash: Visa fits much of Tom Nash's process: revenue rose 15.3% in the first nine months of fiscal 2026, free-cash-flow margin is about 47%, giving a Rule of 40 score near 62, it has beaten EPS estimates every quarter on record here and its 13-category scorecard comes to about 85. It fails his instant-kill rule because debt ($23,858M) exceeds cash ($13,792M), faces the DOJ's debit monopolization lawsuit, and its five-year return slightly trails the S&P 500. On valuation it fails: the price implies about 31% annual growth and his 12% DCF gives roughly $200 a share against about $396, with a PEG of 1.89.

momentum.evidence: Visa's shares rose about 15.3% over the 52 weeks to October 13, 2026 ($396.06), behind the S&P 500 (SPY total return about 20.4%).

g4.evidence: Visa is led by CEO Ryan McInerney (since 2023) and is long held by well-known investors such as Berkshire Hathaway and Akre Capital.

g6.evidence: Commentators often call Visa expensive at about 34 times trailing earnings, though most analysts still rate it a buy.

simple.evidence: Visa earns a small fee on each card payment run over its network and takes no credit risk, a model a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Net revenue rose every year from $21,846M in FY2020 to $40,000M in FY2025, with operating margins near 60% or more throughout.

integrity.evidence: Visa reports clearly, returns most cash through buybacks and dividends (share count down about 2.9% in the past year) and has an independent board, though executive pay is high and the CEO sells shares regularly under trading plans.

b6.evidence: Visa's acquisitions (e.g. Earthport, Tink, Featurespace) are small, bolt-on technology deals tied to its network rather than empire-building.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 55% and ROE about 61%, with total debt of $23,858M modest against about $21B of yearly free cash flow.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow was $21,577M against GAAP net income of $19,853M, a conversion above 100%.

b10.evidence: Visa's market value of about $727B today is far above the earnings it has retained since its 2008 IPO, as profits compounded while it bought back shares.

safety.evidence: At about 34 times trailing and 27 times forward earnings, the share price is not well below a conservative estimate of value.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 27 is high but arguably reasonable for 97% gross margins and low-teens revenue growth.

mu5.evidence: With no credit risk, a duopoly network and near-universal acceptance, the main failure paths are regulation and a shift to account-to-account rails, both slow.

reinvest.evidence: Visa needs little capital, so it returns most profit through buybacks and dividends; reinvestment opportunities in value-added services and new flows are attractive but small relative to cash generated.

ly2.evidence: Visa is a stalwart with fast-grower traits whose story is simple: more of the world's payments move from cash to cards and digital credentials.

ly3.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 34 is well above earnings growth in the low-to-mid teens (EPS $9.73 in FY2024 to $10.20 in FY2025 GAAP).

runway.evidence: Cash and checks still account for trillions of dollars of payments, and Visa is expanding into B2B, Visa Direct, value-added services and agentic commerce.

ly7.evidence: The company keeps reducing its share count (down about 2.9% in a year), but insiders only sold, about $62.9M in the last 12 months, led by CEO McInerney.

ly8.evidence: Visa is one of the most widely owned and analysed stocks in the S&P 500.

fi2.evidence: Visa keeps launching new products such as tokenization, Visa Direct, Visa Intelligent Commerce for AI agents and stablecoin settlement.

fi3.evidence: Technology investment produced widely adopted standards such as contactless payments and network tokens, which underpin value-added-services growth.

fi4.evidence: Visa wins and renews multi-year issuer agreements worldwide, supported by $15,751M of client incentives in FY2025.

longterm.evidence: Management invests in long-horizon bets such as agentic commerce and stablecoin settlement while keeping margins steady.

gr1.evidence: Visa has a market value of about $727B and FY2025 net revenue of $40,000M.

ni10.evidence: Visa has reported a GAAP profit in every one of the last ten fiscal years, from $6,328M in FY2015 to $19,853M in FY2025.

gr4.evidence: Visa has paid dividends only since its 2008 IPO, about 18 years.

eps10.evidence: GAAP diluted EPS rose from $2.58 in FY2015 to $10.20 in FY2025, almost four times.

gr6.evidence: The price of $396.06 is about 42 times average GAAP EPS of FY2023-FY2025 ($8.28, $9.73, $10.20).

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 33.7 times a P/B of about 21.0 gives about 708, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: VisaNet is excellent but not ten times better than Mastercard's network; its edge is scale and acceptance.

timing.evidence: The continued shift to digital, contactless and e-commerce payments, plus early AI-agent and stablecoin payments, favours Visa now.

th3.evidence: Visa grew from BankAmericard in a small US card market into the largest global network and keeps extending into new flows.

team.evidence: Management under Ryan McInerney is capable and experienced, but not an exceptional founder team.

th5.evidence: Thousands of issuing banks and acquirers distribute Visa credentials and acceptance, a sales channel competitors cannot easily copy.

durable.evidence: The network effect is very durable, but real-time payment systems like UPI and Pix, stablecoins and regulation could erode share over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Visa's opportunity is well understood and shared with Mastercard rather than a secret others miss.

trend.evidence: Visa is a leading beneficiary of the secular shift from cash to digital payments and is positioning for AI-agent commerce.

dr1.evidence: Nine-month FY2026 net revenue grew 15.3%, faster than FY2025, and consensus FY2026 revenue sits near $45.8B, but growth is steady rather than sharply accelerating.

dr2.evidence: Value-added services and new flows should keep compounding, but most of this is already expected by the market.

dr4.evidence: Visa benefits from nominal spending growth and inflation, and is little affected by rates since it takes no credit risk, but a slowdown in consumer spending would hurt volumes.

dr6.evidence: Upcoming events include FY2026 results in late October 2026 and progress on agentic commerce and stablecoin settlement, offset by the pending DOJ debit case.

dr7.evidence: Its predictability suits a large position for quality investors, but the valuation limits upside for a concentrated bet.

gm.evidence: Gross margin is about 97.7%, reflecting a network with very low marginal cost.

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is about 2.9% ($21.0B TTM FCF on a $727B market value), fair rather than cheap for its quality and growth.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 24.8, an operating earnings yield of about 4%.

pa2.evidence: Visa is not in a temporary setback; results are at record levels.

pa4.evidence: With no credit risk, high margins and a dominant network, the chance of permanent capital loss in the business is small, though the valuation could compress.

wo1.evidence: Visa is building AI-agent payments and stablecoin settlement, but it is not seen as a leader in AI or blockchain.

wo2.evidence: Its unit costs are already very low; falling costs are not opening up large new demand in the way Wright's Law industries do.

wo3.evidence: Visa combines payments with some AI and digital-asset work, but not several innovation platforms in ARK's sense.

wo4.evidence: Visa's addressable market is large but will not be many times larger within five years.

ac3.evidence: Visa takes no credit risk and owns no commodities; its main external exposures are consumer spending and regulation.

ns1.evidence: Visa keeps most scale savings as margin (operating margin about 60% GAAP) rather than cutting prices for merchants.

ns4.evidence: Visa's network should remain central, but regulation and alternative rails make a clearly stronger position in 10-20 years uncertain.

va2.evidence: Visa solves the large problem of paying and being paid safely and instantly across more than 200 countries and territories.

tn1.evidence: Visa sells into the real secular shift from cash to digital payments and is building agentic-commerce and stablecoin rails, but it is a card network dating from 1958 rather than a company built for AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market sees Visa as a toll road on card payments, and that is largely what it is; its push into value-added services and new flows is well understood.

tn3.evidence: Visa is a roughly $720B US payments network, outside small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups.

tn4.evidence: It passes two of three: net revenue rose every year from $21,846M (FY2020) to $40,000M (FY2025) and it is highly profitable, but debt of $23,858M exceeded cash and investments of $13,792M at June 30, 2026.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive in each of the six quarters to June 2026 ($2,625M to $6,402M), but debt exceeded cash and short-term investments in every one, for example $23,858M vs $13,792M at June 30, 2026.

tn6.evidence: Net revenue rose 15.3% in the nine months to June 30, 2026 ($33,764M vs $29,276M) and 14.4% in the June quarter.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of 15.3% plus a trailing free-cash-flow margin of about 47.2% ($21,013M on $44,488M) gives about 62, well above 40.

tn8.evidence: In the nine months to June 30, 2026 net revenue rose 15.3% while total operating expenses rose 13.0% ($12,916M vs $11,430M).

tn9.evidence: It fails the more-debt-than-cash test ($23,858M vs $13,792M at June 30, 2026), though it passes the rest: a $720B market value, 1.12% short interest, a 61.7% GAAP operating margin, 15% growth, EPS beats every recent quarter and founding in 1958.

tn10.evidence: The US Justice Department's 2024 lawsuit accusing Visa of monopolizing debit payments is pending, alongside merchant interchange litigation and the proposed Credit Card Competition Act.

tn11.evidence: Visa provides a global card network that helps banks, merchants and consumers move money instantly and safely, and charges small per-transaction service, data-processing and cross-border fees; clients choose it for near-universal acceptance across about 5 billion credentials.

tn13.evidence: Total 85 of 130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 5 (15.3%), operating margin 10 (61.7% GAAP), short interest 10 (1.12%), institutional ownership 10 (82.7%), revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return 0 (12.9% a year vs SPY's 13.2%, StockAnalysis), moat 10, CEO 5, recession-proof pricing power 10, secular trend 5, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Net revenue grew every year from FY2021 to FY2025, but GAAP operating margin slipped from 64.5% (FY2020) to 60.0% (FY2025), free cash flow dipped from $19,696M (FY2023) to $18,693M (FY2024) and debt exceeded cash.

tn15.evidence: It passes two of four: interest coverage is about 37x ($20,848M operating income vs $566M interest, nine months to June 2026) and liabilities are 1.69x equity, but assets excluding goodwill ($73,765M) are only 1.24x liabilities ($59,412M) and the current ratio is 0.99.

tn18.evidence: Ryan McInerney has delivered growth (revenue from $32,653M in FY2023 to $40,000M in FY2025) but has been CEO only since February 2023, is not a founder and has sold rather than bought shares on the open market.

tn20.evidence: Visa beat consensus EPS in each of the six quarters to March 2026 (AlphaQuery), for example $3.31 vs $3.09 in fiscal Q2 2026, and reported non-GAAP EPS of $3.32, up 11%, in fiscal Q3 2026.

tn21.evidence: Visa has a single CEO, only small bolt-on acquisitions, no accounting concerns, a steady GAAP operating margin (61.7% vs 61.0% in the nine months to June) and only routine insider sales under trading plans.

tn22.evidence: Visa has $44.5B of trailing revenue, about $21B of free cash flow and a shrinking share count, so it is not a hype trap.

tn24.evidence: Holding the trailing 47.2% FCF margin, a 12% discount rate and 4% terminal growth, the $396.06 price implies about 31% annual revenue growth for five years, double the 15.3% Visa is delivering.

tn25.evidence: With 3-year average revenue growth of 10.9% trimmed to 8.7%, a 55.4% average FCF margin, 4% terminal growth, a 12% discount rate and $10,066M of net debt, value is about $200 per share (about $219 untrimmed), below $396.06.

tn26.evidence: Visa's forward P/E of 27.4 is high and its PEG ratio is 1.89 (StockAnalysis, Oct 2026), above Nash's limit of 1.
